Class Curriculum

java.lang.Object
dev.swordai.core.curriculum.Curriculum
public final class Curriculum extends Object
Tracks which stage the agent is on, decides promotion, and paces the final stage's difficulty.

    • DRILL_RANGE

      public static final int DRILL_RANGE
      The lessons of the crit drills, in the order they are taken (see StageSpec.critDrillPass). In both the fighter's feet and camera are held for it.

      The jump: an opponent that stands still, and every few seconds is somewhere else. Half of the time it is right in the fighter's face: jump, and swing on the way down with the weapon back. The rest of the time it is farther off, at the range a sprint hit is made from or beyond: leave the jump alone; one made there gets no swing and costs. The only thing that tells the two apart beforehand is how large the opponent is on screen.

      Where the jump is wanted is drawn tight on purpose. What a drill teaches becomes a habit, and a habit can be added to but not taken back. In 0.13.1 the jump was wanted anywhere within reach; in a fight the opponent is within reach whenever a sprint hit is on, so it jumped then, and a critical hit knocks nobody back: its combos were gone. Now it starts out jumping only at an opponent in its face, and whether a jump from a little farther pays as well is left to real fights, where taking it up is something it can learn.

      When to jump and when not are taught together, from the first jump on, and that is the point. In 0.13.0 the timing came first, on an opponent that was always in reach, and the range after it. By then jumping was a habit: it jumped on nine ticks in ten wherever it stood. A habit like that cannot be unlearned one tick at a time, because holding back for a tick changes nothing when the next tick jumps anyway; a stand-in for the drill, played by the real network and learner (RangeLessonTest), still jumped at the far opponent on nine ticks in ten after 100,000 steps of the second lesson. Taught together from a fresh jump key, the same stand-in has it in about 55,000 steps.

      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • DRILL_PUNISH

      public static final int DRILL_PUNISH
      The punish crit: an opponent that jumps in for critical hits and stays on top of the fighter. Its hit knocks the fighter up; the swing is kept for the way down, and made then if the opponent is still in reach. No jump key in this one: the only way into the air is the opponent's hit, so every critical hit made here is a punish crit.
      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • KEEP_JUMP_STEPS

      static final int KEEP_JUMP_STEPS
      After the lessons the drills go on, and have to stay passed for the stage to be passed. If this many steps of the jump drill go by without enough hits to judge it by, it has stopped making critical hits there, and that is not passed either.

    • PUNISH_DRILL_TRIAL_HITS

      static final int PUNISH_DRILL_TRIAL_HITS
      The punish drill is only a lesson if the opponent is still in reach when the fighter comes down, at least some of the time. If, over this many hits taken in it, fewer than PUNISH_DRILL_MIN_CHANCE_RATE of them left a punish crit there to be made, the fault is the drill's and not the fighter's: the lesson is left, and said to have been (see critDrillLeft()), rather than holding the fighter in it for ever.

    • SELF_OLD_WIN_RATE

      static final float SELF_OLD_WIN_RATE
      Self-play: to take the newest copy's place, a challenger must also hold its own against the copies from before it: at least this share of at least this many fights against them. A style that beats the newest copy but loses to the ones it replaced would only send the fighters round in a circle.

    • SELF_CRIT_SHARE

      static final float SELF_CRIT_SHARE
      Of those replayed fights, the share that goes to the scripted opponent that jumps in for critical hits. A copy of the fighter crits no more than the fighter does, so without these it could reach the end of the curriculum having hardly met an opponent that does; people who crit do it all the time.

      The same for the push towards S, which has far fewer ticks to go by: the ones right after a hit of a combo with the opponent still within three blocks, and a hit throws the fighter beyond that in a tick or two. With forty asked for, most updates of a fight against a copy of itself had too few and the push stayed where it was (0.14.0: three updates in eighteen moved it).
      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • CLOCK_KEPT_FROM_RULES

      static final int CLOCK_KEPT_FROM_RULES
      See load(Path): runs saved under rules from this version on keep a stage's clock through an update that does not change the stage.
      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • REOPEN_BIAS

      public static final float REOPEN_BIAS
      How firmly a reopened head rests on its default: about one tick in twenty goes the other way.
      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • DRILL_MIN_HITS

      static final int DRILL_MIN_HITS
      Hits landed over the recent window below which it is too early to say whether the agent can combo.

    • judgeSelfPlay

      public Curriculum.SelfPlay judgeSelfPlay()
      Self-play: the winner survives. Once enough fights have been decided, a challenger that is clearly ahead takes the champion's place (and the count starts over against it), and one that has all but stopped winning is replaced by a copy of the champion. Call after every update.

    • recordCritDrills

      public int recordCritDrills(Tally jump, Tally punish)
      What the crit drills since the last update came to: those in which the fighter is held, each kind in its own tally. While the lessons are being taken this passes them, one after the other; after the last, the stage's own fights begin. From then on the drills go on as a share of the fights, and this keeps track of whether they are still passed (see critDrillsKept()).
      Parameters:
      jump - the drills against the opponent that stands still
      punish - the drills against the one that jumps in for critical hits
      Returns:
      the lesson that these passed (or that was left, see critDrillLeft()), or -1

    • jumpNudgeTarget

      public float jumpNudgeTarget()
      The share of the ticks right after a swing on which the current stage wants jump pressed, for as long as it pushes for that: held, then let down to nothing. Zero when it does not push (any more).

    • jumpNudge

      public float jumpNudge()
      How strongly the policy is being pushed towards a jump right after a swing; see JumpNudge. Steered after every update so that the jump is pressed about as often as jumpNudgeTarget() says: if the network leans against jumping, the push grows, so for the time the stage has set aside it cannot unlearn the jump before it has found out what a jump is for.

    • backNudgeTarget

      public float backNudgeTarget()
      The share of the ticks right after a hit of a combo it is taking on which the current stage wants S held, for as long as it pushes for that: held, then let down to nothing.

    • backNudge

      public float backNudge()
      How strongly the policy is being pushed towards S in those ticks; steered like jumpNudge(). See BackNudge.

    • setStage

      Jumps to a stage by hand; progress counters for it start over.

    • fightStageIndex

      public int fightStageIndex()
      The stage whose keys and rewards a fight against a real opponent is played and learned with. A real opponent does everything at once: it combos, it crits. So once the run has reached the stage before the one that has every key, such a fight is played as that one, with every key and with being comboed, getting out and critical hits all paid for. Earlier on, and from that stage onwards, it is played as the stage the run is in.
